opus-5.5.text:
It's fascinating, and honestly a bit surprising the first time you see it. With images, the process feels very intuitive. You start from noise, and first the coarse structure appears, the overall layout and colors, and then progressively finer details get filled in. It mirrors how an artist might sketch first and then refine, so it feels natural.

With text, at least in the discrete diffusion models we've been working on, it looks quite different from what people are used to with autoregressive models. You don't see words appearing one at a time, left to right. You start with a sequence that's essentially all masked or noisy tokens, and then words start popping in at various positions all at once. Often the model commits to some of the more "anchoring" tokens first, structural pieces, key content words, sometimes the end of a sentence before the middle, and then it fills in the connective tissue around them. So in a way there's an analogy to images: there's a coarse-to-fine flavor, where the skeleton of the answer emerges and then the details get resolved.

What I find most interesting is that it gives you a window into how the model is reasoning globally about the whole output rather than committing token by token. It can revise and refine in parallel, and that's precisely where the speed advantages come from, since you're generating many tokens per step instead of one. It also suggests these models might be better at things that require planning or consistency across the whole sequence, because they're not locked into early decisions the way a left-to-right model is.

So images feel more familiar, but text diffusion is, to me, more surprising to watch, because it breaks our intuition that language has to be produced sequentially.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a really different experience, and honestly that difference is part of what got me excited about this direction in the first place.

With images, you start from pure noise, and for the first chunk of the process you're basically looking at static. Then gradually the large-scale structure resolves — you see a blob that might be a face, a horizon line, the rough composition — and the fine details fill in at the very end. It's very coarse-to-fine, and it's visually intuitive. You can almost feel the model "deciding" what the scene is going to be before it commits to the texture.

Text is more interesting to watch, in a way, because text is discrete. There's no such thing as a "slightly noisy" word in the same sense as a slightly noisy pixel. So what you see instead is a kind of sketch of the whole passage appearing at once. Early on, the model fills in the words it's most confident about — often the function words, the structural skeleton, maybe a few key nouns that anchor the topic — and the rest are still masked or jumbled. Then over successive steps, the gaps get resolved in parallel, and the passage sharpens everywhere simultaneously rather than left to right.

The thing that really strikes people the first time they see it is that the ending can show up before the middle. If you ask for a story, you might see the last sentence crystallize fairly early, and then the model works out how to get there. That's fundamentally different from autoregressive generation, where the model has committed to every token in order and can't go back. Diffusion gives you this global view where the model is reasoning about the whole output as a single object, which is why it's good at things like infilling or satisfying constraints at both ends of a document.

So I'd say images feel like a photograph developing, and text feels more like someone solving a crossword puzzle — the easy clues go in first, those constrain the harder ones, and the whole thing resolves together. Both are coarse-to-fine, but for text, "coarse" means semantic confidence rather than spatial scale. Watching that unfold made it click for me that this isn't just a different sampler; it's a different way of thinking about what generating language even is.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s fascinating because we’re so used to seeing text generated from left to right. With diffusion, you can have a rough version of the whole sentence, and then different parts get revised as the process goes on. So it feels a little more like writing and editing a draft.

With images, you can often see the overall structure emerge before the fine details become clear. With text, that progression is harder to interpret. A single word can change the meaning of the entire sentence, so a small local change can have a pretty big effect. But that ability to go back and revise—to make different parts of the output more consistent with one another—is one of the things I find really interesting about this approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s fascinating because, with images, you can see this gradual progression from noise to something recognizable. At first you get the broad structure, and then more and more details emerge. With text, the intermediate states are harder to interpret. You might see some words that make sense locally, but the sentence as a whole doesn’t quite fit together yet. And then, as you refine it, those pieces start to become consistent.

What I find particularly interesting is that you can revise the whole sequence. You’re not committing to the first word and then building everything on top of that decision. You can change something at the beginning based on what’s happening at the end. So watching it emerge gives you a very different intuition about how language can be generated.

r001.rationale: It says image progression is recognizable, while text intermediate states are harder to interpret.
